questions.title: Kafka Consumer Groups and Partitions
questions.question: How do Kafka consumer groups work and how do partitions enable parallel processing?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Consumer group: a group of consumers that jointly consume a topic — each partition assigned to one consumer
- Max parallelism: limited by partition count — adding consumers beyond partition count wastes resources
- Rebalancing: when consumer joins/leaves group, partitions are reassigned — brief pause in consumption
- Offset management: each consumer group tracks its position (offset) per partition independently
- __consumer_offsets: internal Kafka topic storing committed offsets
- Multiple groups: each consumer group reads the topic independently — decoupled subscriptions
- Sticky assignment: preferred partition assignment strategy to minimize rebalances
- Static group membership: reduces rebalances when consumers restart temporarily

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A consumer group lets multiple consumers divide the work of processing a topic. Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer in the group. If you have 6 partitions and 3 consumers, each consumer handles 2 partitions concurrently. This is how Kafka achieves horizontal scalability — you increase partitions and consumers together to increase throughput.

The partition count is the ceiling on parallelism. If you have 6 partitions and 8 consumers in the same group, 2 consumers sit idle because there are no partitions to assign them. Conversely, if you need more throughput from an existing topic, you can increase the partition count — but partitions can only be added, never removed, so plan capacity in advance.

Multiple consumer groups are a powerful pattern. A topic can be consumed by many completely independent groups, each maintaining its own offset. Your order-service can consume the payments topic to update order status, while analytics-service consumes the same topic to update dashboards, and audit-service consumes it for compliance logging. Each group progresses at its own pace without affecting the others.

speakable_v2.hook: A consumer group lets multiple consumers divide the work of processing a topic.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Each group progresses at its own pace without affecting the others.

questions.title: Kafka Error Handling and Dead Letter Topics
questions.question: How do you handle processing failures and implement dead letter queues in Spring Kafka?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Retry: DefaultErrorHandler with BackOff — retry before sending to DLT
- Dead Letter Topic (DLT): failed messages after retries go to {topic}.DLT — inspect, replay, discard
- DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer: publishes failed messages to DLT with original headers
- Non-retryable exceptions: configure to skip retries for certain exceptions (e.g., deserialization errors)
- Backoff: ExponentialBackOff or FixedBackOff — avoid thundering herd on retry
- Poison pill: message that always fails — must not block the partition; DLT solves this
- @RetryableTopic: annotation-based retry with separate retry topics
- Observability: log correlation IDs from event headers for tracing

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The most dangerous failure pattern in Kafka is the poison pill — a message that always causes an exception. Without proper error handling, a consumer that crashes on a poison pill will restart, read the same message, crash again, forever. The partition is effectively blocked.

The solution is a dead letter topic combined with a retry policy. Spring Kafka's DefaultErrorHandler retries the message a configurable number of times with backoff. If it still fails after all retries, the DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer publishes the original message to a dead letter topic, typically named with a .DLT suffix, with headers containing the original topic, partition, offset, and the exception. The consumer then commits the offset and moves on — the partition is unblocked.

The DLT messages can be inspected and triaged manually. If they failed due to a bug in the consumer, you fix the bug, then replay the DLT messages after the fix is deployed. If they were truly invalid data, you discard them after investigation. This separation keeps the main consumer running while giving you full visibility into failures.

speakable_v2.hook: The most dangerous failure pattern in Kafka is the poison pill — a message that always causes an exception.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This separation keeps the main consumer running while giving you full visibility into failures.

questions.title: Kafka Message Ordering and Exactly-Once
questions.question: How does Kafka guarantee message ordering and what are the idempotent producer and exactly-once semantics?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Ordering: guaranteed within a partition, not across partitions
- Partition key: same key → same partition → ordered delivery (e.g., orderId as key)
- Idempotent producer: enable.idempotence=true — broker deduplicates retried messages by producer ID + sequence number
- Exactly-once semantics (EOS): idempotent producer + transactional producer + read_committed isolation
- Transaction: atomically write to multiple partitions and commit consumer offset
- At-least-once (default): possible duplicates — consumer must deduplicate (idempotent consumer)
- At-most-once: acks=0 — possible message loss, no retry
- Delivery guarantees involve trade-offs: throughput vs. safety

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Kafka guarantees ordering within a single partition, not across the whole topic. When you write messages with the same partition key, Kafka always routes them to the same partition, preserving their relative order. For an order processing system, using the order ID as the partition key ensures all events for a given order — created, payment confirmed, shipped — arrive in the correct sequence.

By default Kafka provides at-least-once delivery. If a producer retries after a network failure, the broker might receive the message twice. Enabling enable.idempotence=true on the producer fixes this — the broker tracks a sequence number per producer and silently discards duplicate sends. This gives you exactly-once at the producer-broker boundary.

Full end-to-end exactly-once semantics — covering producer, broker, and consumer — requires Kafka transactions. You configure a transactionalId on the producer, and the consumer sets isolation.level=read_committed. The producer can then atomically write messages to multiple topics and commit consumer offsets in a single transaction. Either everything commits or nothing does. The trade-off is lower throughput and higher latency, so use it only when duplicate processing genuinely can't be tolerated.

speakable_v2.hook: Kafka guarantees ordering within a single partition, not across the whole topic.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: The trade-off is lower throughput and higher latency, so use it only when duplicate processing genuinely can't be tolerated.

questions.title: Kafka Custom Partitioners and Routing
questions.question: When and how do you use custom Kafka partitioners to control message routing?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Default: round-robin for null keys; hash(key) % numPartitions for keyed messages
- Custom partitioner: implements Partitioner interface — determine partition for each record
- Use cases: geographic routing, priority lanes, tenant isolation, sticky routing
- Key-based: default hash works for simple key→partition mapping
- Sticky partitioner (default since Kafka 2.4): batch records to same partition until full — better throughput
- UniformStickyPartitioner: improved batching for null-key messages
- Hot partition: common problem when one key dominates — custom partitioner can distribute

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Kafka's default partitioner routes keyed messages by hash of the key modulo partition count. This guarantees that all messages with the same key go to the same partition, ensuring ordering for that key. For most use cases, this is exactly what you want — all events for the same order ID go to the same partition, processed in order.

Custom partitioners become necessary when you have specific routing requirements the default doesn't handle. For example, if you need VIP tenant messages to go to dedicated partitions for priority processing, or if you want geographic routing where European user events go to partitions consumed by European processors.

Hot partitions are the main problem to watch for. If one key generates far more messages than others — like a very active user or a high-volume tenant — all their messages pile up in one partition while others are underutilized. A custom partitioner can detect hot keys and spread their messages across multiple partitions, though you lose the ordering guarantee for that key.

questions.title: Kafka Connect and Change Data Capture
questions.question: What is Kafka Connect and how do you use Change Data Capture with Debezium?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Kafka Connect: framework for streaming data between Kafka and other systems
- Source connector: reads from external system → writes to Kafka (DB, S3, APIs)
- Sink connector: reads from Kafka → writes to external system (Elasticsearch, S3, BigQuery)
- Debezium: CDC source connector — reads PostgreSQL/MySQL WAL → streams all row changes to Kafka
- CDC events: INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE with before/after row state
- Use cases: sync to search index, event sourcing, audit log, cache invalidation, replication
- At-least-once: exactly-once delivery with sink idempotent writes
- Avro + Schema Registry: strongly typed events with schema evolution

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Kafka Connect is a framework for moving data reliably between Kafka and other systems without writing custom producer/consumer code. Source connectors pull data from a system into Kafka, sink connectors push data from Kafka into a system. There are hundreds of community connectors for databases, cloud storage, search engines, and more.

Debezium is the most important source connector for Java backend teams. It reads the PostgreSQL write-ahead log and publishes every row change — insert, update, delete — as a structured Kafka event containing the before and after state of the row. This enables Change Data Capture: any change to your database automatically becomes a Kafka event, without modifying the application code that made the change.

The primary use cases for CDC are keeping downstream systems synchronized — like updating an Elasticsearch search index when products change in PostgreSQL — and the transactional outbox pattern where Debezium publishes database events that other services consume. CDC is more reliable than polling because it captures every change atomically with the original transaction.

speakable_v2.hook: Kafka Connect is a framework for moving data reliably between Kafka and other systems without writing custom producer/consumer code.

speakable_v2.cap: CDC is more reliable than polling because it captures every change atomically with the original transaction.

questions.title: Kafka Schema Registry and Avro Serialization
questions.question: What is the Kafka Schema Registry and why should you use Avro instead of plain JSON?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Schema Registry: centralized schema store for Kafka topics — prevents incompatible schema changes
- Avro: binary format with schema — compact, fast, supports schema evolution
- JSON: human-readable but no schema enforcement — silent breakage when fields change
- Compatibility modes: BACKWARD (new schema can read old data), FORWARD (old schema reads new data), FULL
- Spring Kafka + Confluent Avro: KafkaAvroSerializer/Deserializer auto-registers schemas
- Schema evolution: add optional fields safely (BACKWARD compatible)
- Breaking change: removing required fields or changing types — blocked by Schema Registry

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
JSON is convenient for prototyping but fragile in production. If a producer removes a field that consumers depend on, there's no compile-time error — consumers silently start getting null values and may fail in unexpected ways. Schema Registry with Avro solves this by enforcing schema compatibility at publish time.

Avro stores data in a compact binary format with the schema referenced by an ID. Messages are smaller than JSON — typically 50-70% smaller — and faster to serialize and deserialize. The schema is stored in the Schema Registry, not in every message, so consumers always know the exact structure.

The compatibility mode is the key governance feature. BACKWARD compatibility means new consumer code can still read old messages — you can add new optional fields. FORWARD compatibility means old consumer code can still read new messages. FULL means both. The Schema Registry rejects a schema update that would break the configured compatibility, preventing silent breaking changes between microservices.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Avro Schema

```json
// src/main/avro/OrderCreatedEvent.avsc
{
  "type": "record",
  "name": "OrderCreatedEvent",
  "namespace": "com.myapp.events",
  "fields": [
    {"name": "orderId",   "type": "string"},
    {"name": "userId",    "type": "string"},
    {"name": "totalAmount", "type": "double"},
    {"name": "currency",  "type": "string", "default": "USD"},
    {"name": "items",     "type": {"type": "array", "items": {
      "type": "record",
      "name": "OrderItem",
      "fields": [
        {"name": "productId", "type": "string"},
        {"name": "quantity",  "type": "int"},
        {"name": "price",     "type": "double"}
      ]
    }}},
    // Safe schema evolution: add new optional field with default
    {"name": "couponCode", "type": ["null", "string"], "default": null}
  ]
}
```

## Spring Kafka + Avro Configuration

```yaml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka:9092
    producer:
      value-serializer: io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroSerializer
      properties:
        schema.registry.url: http://schema-registry:8081
    consumer:
      value-deserializer: io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroDeserializer
      properties:
        schema.registry.url: http://schema-registry:8081
        specific.avro.reader: true  # use generated Java classes, not GenericRecord
```

## Producer (Generated Avro Class)

```java
// Maven/Gradle avro plugin generates Java class from .avsc
@Service
public class OrderProducer {
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderCreatedEvent> kafkaTemplate;

    public void publishOrderCreated(Order order) {
        // Generated Avro class — type-safe, validated against schema
        OrderCreatedEvent event = OrderCreatedEvent.newBuilder()
            .setOrderId(order.getId().toString())
            .setUserId(order.getUserId().toString())
            .setTotalAmount(order.getTotal().doubleValue())
            .setCurrency("USD")
            .setItems(order.getItems().stream()
                .map(i -> OrderItem.newBuilder()
                    .setProductId(i.getProductId().toString())
                    .setQuantity(i.getQuantity())
                    .setPrice(i.getPrice().doubleValue())
                    .build())
                .toList())
            .build();

        kafkaTemplate.send("orders.created", order.getId().toString(), event);
        // Avro serializer: registers schema, encodes as binary with schema ID prefix
    }
}
```

## Schema Compatibility

```
BACKWARD (recommended default):
  - New schema can read messages written with old schema
  - Safe changes: add field with default, remove optional field
  - Breaking: remove required field, change type

FORWARD:
  - Old schema can read messages written with new schema
  - Useful when some consumers haven't been updated yet

FULL = BACKWARD + FORWARD
  - Most restrictive — only add/remove optional fields

Schema Registry rejects incompatible schema changes at registration time
→ CI/CD pipeline catches breaking changes before they reach production
```

speakable_v2.hook: JSON is convenient for prototyping but fragile in production.
speakable_v2.cap: The Schema Registry rejects a schema update that would break the configured compatibility, preventing silent breaking changes between microservices.
